title: Claim, Warrant, Impact
subtitle: Argument Foundations · Mission 03
tagline: Every argument that {{cyan:wins}} has three parts. Every argument that {{amber:loses}} is missing one of them.

slides.headline: 30 SECONDS TO SAVE RECESS
body: Your principal just announced: *"We're canceling recess. Forever."*
You have **30 seconds** to change their mind. What do you say?
Whatever just popped into your head — congratulations, that's an {{cyan: argument}}. But was it a *good* one? Would it actually beat a principal who's already made up their mind?
Today you learn the three-part recipe that turns a good idea into an argument that {{amber: actually wins}}.

quote.text: An argument is not the same thing as a contradiction. An argument is a connected series of statements intended to establish a definite proposition.
quote.cite: Monty Python (yes, really) — and also every debate judge ever

items.label: Identify the three parts of a complete argument
Spot what's missing when an argument falls flat
Build your own {{cyan: Claim → Warrant → Impact}} chain

slides.definition: In debate, an {{cyan: argument}} is a complete unit of reasoning made of three parts: a `claim` (what you believe), a `warrant` (why it's true), and an `impact` (why anyone should care).
slides.plainWords: Not a fight. Not just an opinion. A *case* you build, piece by piece, so a judge can follow your logic from "here's what I think" all the way to "here's why it matters."
slides.analogy: Think of it as a **sandwich**. The {{cyan: claim}} is the top bun. The {{amber: warrant}} is the filling — the meat, cheese, whatever makes it worth eating. The {{cyan: impact}} is the bottom bun holding it all up. Take any layer out and the whole thing collapses in your hands.

slides.headline: THE ARGUMENT SANDWICH
slides.intro: Three layers. Every winning argument has all three. Learn to spot them — and learn what your argument is missing when it isn't landing.

cards.name: CLAIM
cards.description: The {{cyan: big idea}} you're defending. One sentence. Take a side.

cards.name: WARRANT
cards.description: The {{amber: reason or evidence}} that makes your claim true. *Why* should anyone believe you?

example.label: Sounds like
example.text: "…because studies show students focus better after physical activity…"

cards.name: IMPACT
cards.description: Why your claim {{cyan: matters}}. What happens in the real world if you're right — or if no one listens?

example.label: Sounds like
example.text: "…which means better test scores and happier students."

slides.headline: WHAT BREAKS WHEN A LAYER IS MISSING
slides.intro: Half the arguments you'll hear in real life — and in debate rounds — are missing a layer. Learn to diagnose them in your opponents *and* in yourself.

rows.name: Claim only
rows.description: Just a statement, no reason. This is {{amber: an opinion}} — not an argument.

counter.label: Example
counter.text: *"Pizza is the best food."* — Cool. Why? Says who? You haven't given anyone a reason to agree.

rows.name: Claim + Warrant, no Impact
rows.description: You've explained *why* it's true, but not *why it matters*. This is {{amber: a fun fact}} — interesting, not persuasive.

counter.label: Example
counter.text: *"Recess helps students focus because exercise increases blood flow to the brain."* — Okay… so what? The judge needs to know what's at stake.

rows.name: Warrant + Impact, no Claim
rows.description: You're rambling about reasons and consequences, but you never said what you actually believe. The judge can't vote for a position you didn't take.

counter.label: Example
counter.text: *"Exercise helps focus, and focused students get better grades."* — Great. What are you arguing *for*? Pick a side.

prompt.label: QUICK CHECK
prompt.question: What are the three parts of a complete argument?

correct.title: ✓ TARGET ACQUIRED
body: Locked in. Every complete argument has a {{cyan: claim}} (your big idea), a {{amber: warrant}} (your reason), and a {{cyan: impact}} (why it matters).
correct.followup: **Pro move:** When you're prepping a speech, write out C-W-I in three separate lines *before* you write any sentences. It forces you to actually have all three.

a.title: ✕ CLOSE — BUT NOT THE LANGUAGE WE USE
body: "Opinion, evidence, conclusion" is what an English teacher might say. In debate, we use {{cyan: claim, warrant, impact}} — same idea, sharper words.
a.followup: **Why it matters:** Saying "opinion" makes your side sound weak. *Claim* sounds like you're staking a position. Words shape how the judge hears you.

c.title: ✕ THAT'S AN ESSAY STRUCTURE
body: Topic / thesis / summary is the shape of a *paper*. An argument is a smaller, sharper thing: {{cyan: claim}}, {{amber: warrant}}, {{cyan: impact}}.

d.title: ✕ THAT'S A DEBATE *EXCHANGE*
body: Question / answer / rebuttal describes a *round* — two debaters going back and forth. The argument itself, the thing each debater builds, is {{cyan: claim, warrant, impact}}.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE — RECALIBRATE
body: The answer is {{cyan: B — Claim, Warrant, Impact}}. Memorize those three words. They're the backbone of every speech you'll give this summer.

prompt.label: FIELD SORT
prompt.scenario: Here's a real argument, broken into three pieces. Sort each piece into the right bin.
prompt.question: Drop each statement into the part of the argument it belongs to.

cards.text: A survey found 82% of students say they express their personality through what they wear.
Less creativity leads to less classroom engagement, which lowers grades over time.

correct.title: ✓ ARGUMENT ASSEMBLED
body: Clean sort. Notice the *shape*: the {{cyan: claim}} takes a side, the {{amber: warrant}} backs it with data, the {{cyan: impact}} tells the judge what's at stake.
correct.followup: **Read the chain out loud:** "Uniforms hurt creativity, *because* 82% of students express themselves through clothes, *which means* less engagement and lower grades." That's a winning structure.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ ARGUMENT MISALIGNED
body: Try this litmus test: ask {{cyan: "What am I claiming?"}} (the big idea), {{amber: "Why is that true?"}} (the reason or data), and {{cyan: "So what?"}} (why it matters).
The statement with a *percentage* or *study* is almost always a **warrant**. The statement about *consequences* — what happens because of the claim — is the **impact**.

prompt.label: DIAGNOSTIC
prompt.scenario: A debater stands up and says: *"Pizza is the best food. Therefore, the cafeteria should serve it every day."*
prompt.question: Which part of the argument is missing?

correct.title: ✓ DIAGNOSIS CONFIRMED
body: Right — there's no {{amber: warrant}}. *Why* is pizza the best? Says who? Without a reason, the claim is just a personal preference dressed up as an argument.
correct.followup: **Field move:** When an opponent does this, your cross-ex question writes itself: *"What's your warrant?"* Watch them squirm.

a.title: ✕ THE CLAIM IS RIGHT THERE
body: *"Pizza is the best food"* and *"the cafeteria should serve it every day"* are both claims — the speaker took a position. What's missing is the {{amber: warrant}}: *why* should anyone believe them?

c.title: ✕ THE IMPACT IS ARGUABLY THERE
body: You could read *"the cafeteria should serve it every day"* as a real-world consequence — a weak impact, but an impact. The clearest missing piece is the {{amber: warrant}}. Why is pizza the best in the first place?

d.title: ✕ NOT COMPLETE
body: There's no reason given. "Pizza is the best" is an *assertion*, not a warranted argument. A judge would call this {{amber: unwarranted}} and move on.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan: B — the warrant}}. The speaker said *what* they believe but never *why*. No reason = no warrant = no real argument.

prompt.label: PATTERN MATCH
prompt.scenario: Match each example statement to which part of the argument it is.
prompt.question: Drag from the left to its match on the right.

items.text: "Cell phones should be banned in class."
"…because a Stanford study found phones cut focus time in half."
"…which means lower test scores and weaker college applications."
IMPACT — why it matters in the real world

correct.title: ✓ PATTERN LOCKED
body: Read it as one chain: *"Phones should be banned, **because** Stanford shows they cut focus in half, **which means** lower scores and worse college outcomes."* That's a {{cyan: complete}} argument.
correct.followup: **Bridge words to memorize:** `because` signals a **warrant** is coming. `which means` or `so` signals an **impact** is coming. Use them out loud — judges flow what they hear, not what you meant.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ CHAIN BROKEN
body: Use the bridge words as your tell: a statement after {{amber: "because"}} is almost always a **warrant**. A statement after {{cyan: "which means"}} or {{cyan: "so"}} is almost always an **impact**. The opening position — the thing you're defending — is the **claim**.

prompt.label: BUILD ORDER
prompt.scenario: You're putting together an argument about school start times. Fill in the missing labels for each part.
prompt.question: Drop the right word into each blank.

slides.template:
Schools should start later in the morning. → This is the {{1}}.
Because teenagers' brains don't fully wake up until 10am, according to sleep research. → This is the {{2}}.
Which means students who start later get better grades, fewer car accidents, and better mental health. → This is the {{3}}.

blanks.hint: The big idea — the position being taken
Why it matters in the real world

correct.title: ✓ ARGUMENT BUILT
body: Nicely sequenced. Notice the bridge words again: {{amber: "because"}} signals a warrant. {{cyan: "which means"}} signals an impact. Train your ear to hear them and you'll diagnose any argument in seconds.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ REBUILD
body: Three checkpoints: {{cyan: claim}} = the position. {{amber: warrant}} = the reason (usually follows *because*). {{cyan: impact}} = the consequence (usually follows *which means* or *so*).

prompt.label: JUDGE'S CHAIR
prompt.scenario: Two debaters give the same claim and warrant. Only one adds an {{cyan: impact}}.
prompt.question: Why does the one with an impact usually win the ballot?

options.text: Because the impact tells the judge what's at stake — it gives them a reason to vote
Because impacts add more vocabulary words
Because judges aren't allowed to vote without an impact

correct.title: ✓ THAT'S THE WHOLE GAME
body: Exactly. A judge isn't voting on who has the prettiest argument — they're voting on {{cyan: what matters more}}. No impact, no stakes, no reason to vote your way.
correct.followup: **Pro tip:** The biggest impacts win rounds. *"Students get slightly worse grades"* is an impact, sure. *"Students fall behind, drop out, and the achievement gap widens"* is a **bigger** impact. Always ask: *can I push this further?*

a.title: ✕ LENGTH ISN'T THE POINT
body: Long speeches can absolutely lose. What wins is {{cyan: stakes}} — telling the judge *what happens* if your side is right. That's the impact's job.

c.title: ✕ NOT ABOUT VOCAB
body: The impact isn't decoration — it's the *reason to vote*. Without it, the judge is left thinking "okay… and?" Always answer the *so what*.

d.title: ✕ JUDGES *CAN* VOTE, BUT THEY USUALLY WON'T FOR YOU
body: Nothing in the rules forbids it. But judges weigh arguments by {{cyan: impact size}}. If your opponent shows real-world consequences and you don't, they get the ballot.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan: B}}. The impact gives the judge *stakes* — a reason your side matters in the real world. No impact, no win.

slides.headline: ARGUMENT SANDWICH: ASSEMBLED
slides.subtext: You now have the recipe every winning debater uses. {{cyan: Claim}} → {{amber: Warrant}} → {{cyan: Impact}}. Use it in every speech, every cross-ex answer, every rebuttal — until it's automatic.
